marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q019.takeaway: Inferior occipitotemporal damage can cause prosopagnosia.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q019.displayText: Prosopagnosia is inability to recognize familiar faces despite intact vision and recognition of other objects. It is associated especially with the inferior occipitotemporal region, often right-dominant in right-handed individuals; patients may recognize people by voice or show an autonomic response without consciously identifying a face.

rationales.a: Frontal injury can impair judgment/executive behavior, but face-recognition failure localizes to occipitotemporal regions.
rationales.b: Occipital lesions can impair visual processing generally; prosopagnosia is more specifically linked to inferior occipitotemporal cortex.
rationales.c: Posterior parietal lesions cause spatial/attention deficits; face recognition is represented in inferior temporal-occipital regions.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q020.takeaway: Forward digit span is the best immediate-memory test among these options.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q020.displayText: Immediate memory is assessed with forward digit span, testing attention and short-term retention. The source’s normal range is about seven digits (±2), with two skips allowed. Backward digit span is harder and assesses working manipulation; serial 100-minus-7 subtraction mainly tests concentration.

rationales.b: Serial sevens primarily test concentration and calculation, not immediate span.
rationales.c: Backward digit span adds working-memory manipulation and is not the source’s best immediate-memory test.
rationales.d: Serial subtraction from 20 is not a digit-span test and does not assess immediate retention as directly.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q021.takeaway: Mixed EEG, eye movements, and reduced muscle tone identify REM sleep.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q021.displayText: The marked polysomnography interval is REM sleep: EOG shows positive eye movements, EEG has mixed/activated frequencies, and EMG tone is minimal. The source’s comparison table distinguishes active wakefulness (fast EEG, positive EOG, positive EMG), REM (mixed EEG, positive EOG, reduced EMG), and NREM (slow EEG, no rapid eye movements, preserved tone).

rationales.b: N1 is light NREM with transition activity; the combination of rapid eye movements and atonia marks REM.
rationales.c: N2 includes sleep spindles and K complexes and lacks the marked REM eye-movement/low-EMG pattern.
rationales.d: N3 has slow delta EEG and preserved muscle tone rather than activated mixed EEG with REM atonia.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q022.takeaway: The source places sleep-related bruxism most often in NREM stage 2.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q022.displayText: Sleep-related bruxism is grinding or clenching teeth during sleep and is most common in NREM stage 2 in the source classification. It is a parasomnia; staging is based on sleep physiology rather than the waking time when the behavior is noticed.

rationales.b: NREM 3 is deep slow-wave sleep and is associated with disorders such as night terrors and sleepwalking in this source set.
rationales.c: The source associates bruxism with NREM 2, not REM sleep.
rationales.d: Stage 4 is an older deep-NREM designation, not the source’s stage for bruxism.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q023.takeaway: Bruxism is associated with NREM 2 rather than stage 3.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q023.displayText: Night terrors, nocturnal enuresis, and sleepwalking are associated with deep NREM stage 3 in this question set. Bruxism is more common in NREM stage 2, so it is the listed disorder that does not occur in stage 3.

rationales.a: Night terrors are a classic deep-NREM parasomnia and can occur in stage 3.
rationales.b: Nocturnal enuresis is included among stage-3 sleep disorders in the source grouping.
rationales.d: Sleepwalking commonly arises from deep NREM sleep, unlike stage-2 bruxism.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q024.takeaway: Hippocampal injury can prevent formation of new long-term memories.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q024.displayText: Anterograde amnesia after injury means impaired formation of new long-term memories. The hippocampus is essential for converting recent experiences into durable memories; it does not serve as the permanent store for all established memories, so existing remote memories may remain accessible.

rationales.a: Amygdala contributes to emotional learning but is not the primary structure for general memory consolidation in this case.
rationales.b: Neocortex stores established long-term memories; the new-memory consolidation deficit points to hippocampus.
rationales.d: Hypothalamus regulates autonomic/endocrine functions, not the primary declarative-memory consolidation process.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q025.takeaway: Medial temporal lobe is correctly paired with declarative memory.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q025.displayText: Declarative memory—conscious recall of facts and events—depends on medial temporal-lobe structures, including hippocampus, for encoding and retention. Priming is associated with neocortex, procedural skills with striatum, and associative emotional or motor learning with amygdala or cerebellum.

rationales.a: Associative learning is linked to amygdala/cerebellum in the source, while neocortex is specifically paired with priming.
rationales.c: Angular gyrus is not the procedural-memory substrate; procedural skills/habits involve striatum.
rationales.d: Striatum supports procedural learning; priming is associated with neocortex.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q026.takeaway: Bilateral frontal injury commonly impairs judgment.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q026.displayText: Frontal-lobe injury can impair executive functions, motivation, attention, sequencing, judgment, and personality. The vignette’s severe bilateral injury would make preserved judgment least likely; other possible features include slowed thinking, reduced curiosity, social withdrawal, irritability, and incontinence.

rationales.a: Slowed thinking can occur with frontal-lobe syndrome, so it is plausible after this injury.
rationales.b: Decreased curiosity is one of the source-listed frontal-lobe effects.
rationales.c: Social withdrawal is also associated with frontal-lobe injury; preserved judgment is the least likely feature.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q027.takeaway: Inferior frontal-gyrus injury can cause Broca motor aphasia.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q027.displayText: The inferior frontal gyrus contains Broca’s motor-speech area. A lesion causes nonfluent, effortful speech with word-finding pauses and reduced function words, while comprehension is relatively intact; patients know what they want to say but cannot readily produce it.

rationales.b: Wernicke’s area lies in posterior superior temporal gyrus and supports comprehension, not the inferior frontal lesion site.
rationales.c: Primary auditory cortex is in temporal lobe; this injury localizes to frontal motor-speech area.
rationales.d: Visual cortex is occipital, not inferior frontal.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q028.takeaway: Prosopagnosia is impaired recognition of known faces.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q028.displayText: Prosopagnosia means difficulty identifying familiar faces. It is linked particularly to right inferior temporal/occipitotemporal regions in many right-handed people; patients may still recognize objects, reproduce forms, or identify people by voice.

rationales.a: Impaired consciousness is not the specific face-recognition deficit named by prosopagnosia.
rationales.b: Lack of awareness of one’s own problems describes anosognosia, not prosopagnosia.
rationales.d: Failure to identify objects is object agnosia; prosopagnosia specifically concerns faces.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q029.takeaway: Frontal-lobe circuits regulate emotional expression and behavior.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q029.displayText: The frontal lobe regulates and controls emotional expression, while the limbic system—especially amygdala—generates emotional salience and ratings and directs hypothalamic autonomic/endocrine responses. The frontal cortex provides top-down regulation of emotional behavior.

rationales.a: The temporal lobe contains limbic structures involved in emotion, but the keyed regulatory control is frontal.
rationales.c: The limbic system generates and assigns emotional significance; frontal-lobe circuits regulate expression.
rationales.d: Parietal lobe is primarily somatosensory and spatial, not the main emotion-regulation region.
